title: Precious Artifact
description: 'Precious Artifact' appeared in Galaxy Magazine for October 1964 and was collected in We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990) and in later volumes of Dick's collected stories. It is one of the handful of stories Dick wrote in 1964, the year in which he produced 'Oh, to Be a Blobel!', 'The Little Black Box' and 'Cantata 140', and it belongs to his early-1960s manner: a small-time professional - here a man who rebuilds and repairs the machines of a ruined civilisation - discovers that the world he is trying to restore is not the world that existed, and that the artefact he has been preserving is a record of somebody else's catastrophe.
plot_or_argument: 'Precious Artifact' is a story about restoration as a form of remembering, and it works by withholding the nature of the object until the protagonist has already committed himself to recovering it. Dick's ruined Earth is described with the flatness of a man describing his own backyard: the salvage is ordinary work, the machinery is ordinary machinery, and the war that made the ruins is reported as a fact of the trade rather than as a catastrophe. The arrival of the off-world visitor introduces the political question, and the story's turn is the discovery that the artefact is a piece of evidence - that the history of the war has been rewritten by the side that won, and that the object the protagonist has been paid to find will contradict the official account. The ending is characteristically Dick: it does not stage a trial or a revelation, but leaves the protagonist with a decision he makes alone and for reasons the story only partly explains, so that the reader is left with the sense that the moral question has been answered privately rather than publicly.
narrative_structure: A single linear narrative in the third person, following the protagonist through one commission from the arrival of the visitor to the disposal of the artefact; the backstory of the war is given in dialogue and in the protagonist's own recollection rather than in exposition.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, rapid, colloquial American prose with a heavy proportion of dialogue; technical vocabulary used casually and without explanation, so that the reader learns the world from the trade; a deadpan tone applied to grotesque or apocalyptic material; and an ending that closes the action without explaining the protagonist's motive.
historical_context: Published in Galaxy Magazine for October 1964, in the middle of the most productive decade of Dick's career and in the year of 'Oh, to Be a Blobel!', 'The Little Black Box', 'Cantata 140' and 'A Game of Unchance'. It was collected in We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990) and in The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick. Its ruined-Earth setting belongs to the postwar science-fiction tradition of the aftermath narrative, and its concern with the politics of the record belongs to the Cold War culture of the early 1960s.
literary_significance: 'Precious Artifact' is a representative rather than a famous Dick story, and it is valuable precisely for that: it shows his characteristic procedures - the working protagonist, the object that carries a suppressed history, the flat tone applied to catastrophe - at short-story length. It is included in the standard collected editions of his stories and is used in criticism to illustrate the 1964 phase of his work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Galaxy Magazine, October 1964; collected in We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990) and in The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick, vol. 2. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story's first subject is the artefact as a carrier of memory - the object that survives a catastrophe and tells a different story from the one the survivors tell. Its second is the ordinary worker inside a ruined economy, whose trade keeps him alive and also implicates him in the lies of his customers. The third is the politics of the record: who owns the history of a war, and what the victor does to the evidence. The fourth is Dick's recurring question of the false world - the sense that the reality one inhabits has been constructed for someone else's convenience - which this story poses in the modest form of a piece of salvage rather than a cosmic vision.
summary: The story is set on a depopulated and ruined Earth in the aftermath of a war between human settlements on other planets, and its protagonist makes his living by salvaging and repairing the mechanical and electronic remains of the old civilisation - the 'precious artifacts' of the title. He is visited by an agent or investigator from one of the off-world colonies, who wants a particular object recovered from the ruins; the object turns out to be a recording or a data store that contains the history of the war and, in particular, the fact that the colony the visitor represents was responsible for the destruction of the Earth. The protagonist's trade - the careful restoration of broken things - becomes the story's moral centre, since what he recovers is not a piece of machinery but a truth that the purchaser would rather have left in the rubble. The story ends with the artefact in the hands of someone who understands what it is, and with the protagonist's small, compromised decision about what to do with it.
critical_context: Criticism of Dick's short fiction places the 1964 stories in the phase between the realist novels of the late 1950s and the metaphysical novels after 1965, and reads 'Precious Artifact' as an early instance of his interest in the manufactured record and in the politics of memory; the story is discussed more often in surveys of his career than in single-author studies.
research_notes: The Galaxy printing of October 1964 is recorded from the FictionMags Index and from the finding aid of the Philip K. Dick collection at the University of California; the story's first book collection is given as We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990). No printed bibliography of Dick was consulted.

title: Schrödinger's Cat
description: 'Schrodinger's Cat' was first published in Universe 5 (1974), the anthology edited by Terry Carr, and collected in The Compass Rose (1982) and in Buffalo Gals and Other Animal Presences (1987). A narrator in a house in the American countryside is visited, in quick succession, by a cat, by a dog-like creature carrying a knapsack, a box and a photon gun, and by a series of further visitors, each of whom explains the quantum-mechanical thought experiment that gives the story its title. The story is a comedy of explanation and a parable about observation: the cat in the box is neither alive nor dead until someone opens the lid, and the narrator discovers that the same is true of the world she is standing in.
plot_or_argument: 'Schrodinger's Cat' is a story about the moment before a decision, and its method is escalation. Each visitor explains the experiment more fully and less helpfully than the last; the box stays closed; and the narrator, who is the only person in the story with the power to open it, becomes increasingly unable to act. Le Guin's prose is comic and exact - the dog is earnest, the cat is insufferable, the narrator is put-upon - and the comedy carries a genuine philosophical question: if observation is what makes a thing determinate, then the observer is part of the experiment, and there is no position outside it from which to decide. The story's final movement, in which the house is opened from above by something vast, extends the joke one level further: the narrator is herself a cat in a box, and the reader is the observer who has been waiting for her to act. It is one of the small number of stories credited with bringing Schrodinger's thought experiment into popular culture, and it does so not by explaining the physics but by making the reader feel the vertigo of the position.
narrative_structure: A single continuous first-person narration in the present tense, built as a series of arrivals at the narrator's house; each arrival adds a layer of explanation, and the story escalates from the domestic to the cosmic without a scene break.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, dry, comic first-person prose in the present tense; short paragraphs and quick beats; a domestic vocabulary set against the technical vocabulary of quantum mechanics; and dialogue in which each speaker is characterised by the way he explains.
historical_context: Written in September 1972 and first published in Universe 5 (1974), edited by Terry Carr, then collected in The Compass Rose (1982) and Buffalo Gals and Other Animal Presences (1987). Le Guin had learned of the thought experiment while researching quantum mechanics for The Dispossessed (1974), and the story is credited by historians of science with helping to bring Schrodinger's cat into popular culture in the 1970s and 1980s.
literary_significance: 'Schrodinger's Cat' is the story most often credited with popularising Schrodinger's thought experiment outside physics, and it is a standard example of Le Guin's comic mode; it is anthologised in collections of science fiction and of writing about science, and it is used in teaching to show how a philosophical problem can be dramatised rather than explained.
bibliographical_notes: Written September 1972; first published in Universe 5, ed. Terry Carr (1974); collected in The Compass Rose (1982) and Buffalo Gals and Other Animal Presences (1987). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story's first subject is observation and determinacy - the proposition that a thing is not settled until it is seen, and the corollary that the observer is never outside the system she observes. Its second is the comedy of explanation: every visitor arrives with a theory, and the theories multiply rather than resolve. The third is the ordinary domestic setting - the house, the doorbell, the cat on the sofa - used as the stage for a metaphysical crisis, which is Le Guin's characteristic way of making abstraction habitable. The fourth is the anthropologist's interest in how other minds model the world: the dog is a reasoner, the cat is a fact, and the narrator is the field in which their models collide.
summary: The story begins with the narrator noticing that 'things appear to be coming to some sort of climax': a cat has arrived in her house and will not leave. The doorbell rings, and a creature that looks like a dog - large, earnest, carrying a huge knapsack - enters and begins to unpack: a box, a photon gun, and the apparatus of an experiment. The dog recognises the cat as 'Schrodinger's cat' and explains the thought experiment: a cat sealed in a box with a device that may or may not kill it is, according to quantum mechanics, neither alive nor dead until the box is opened and the outcome observed. The cat, obligingly, jumps into the box and closes the lid with its tail, and the narrator is left with the decision of whether to open it. Before she can, a series of further visitors arrives - each with a different account of the experiment and of what the narrator ought to do - and the house itself begins to come apart, the roof being removed by something larger than the story can name. The story ends with the narrator's recognition that she is inside a thought experiment and that her own observation is what the experiment is waiting for.
critical_context: Critics have read the story as a comedy of the observer problem, as an instance of Le Guin's interest in the models by which minds construe the world, and as a companion to 'The Author of the Acacia Seeds' in its play with non-human perspectives; historians of science have cited it in accounts of how the thought experiment entered popular culture, and Le Guin herself called it a 'slight, playful story with an undercurrent of sorrow'.
research_notes: The date of 1974 in the list is the date of first publication in Universe 5, not of composition; the story was finished in September 1972. The anthology's copyright page gives the 1974 first appearance, and the several published accounts of the story agree on it.

title: Bloodchild
description: 'Bloodchild' was first published in Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine for June 1984 and won the Hugo, the Nebula, the Locus and the Science Fiction Chronicle awards for best novelette; it became the title story of Butler's collection Bloodchild and Other Stories (1995). It is narrated by Gan, a young human man living on a reservation on an alien world governed by the Tlic, a large insect-like species that needs human bodies to carry its young. The story is usually described as a story about male pregnancy, and Butler insisted that it was a love story: a story about what a person will consent to for the sake of the people he loves, and about the price of a bargain that keeps both species alive.
plot_or_argument: 'Bloodchild' is a story about a bargain, and its achievement is to make the bargain feel simultaneously monstrous and reasonable. The Tlic need human bodies to reproduce, and humans need the Tlic for protection and for the eggs that make life bearable; the arrangement is slavery in one reading and symbiosis in another, and Butler refuses to settle it. Gan's narration is calm, exact and loving: he describes T'Gatoi's limbs and her smell with affection, and he describes the operation on Bram Lomas with the same flat attention, so that the reader cannot separate the tenderness from the horror. The story's turning point is not the operation but Gan's decision afterwards, which he makes not out of submission but out of a clear-eyed calculation about what he can bear and what his family needs. Butler said that readers who took the story as an allegory of slavery had missed what she meant, and that she had written a love story about a man who chooses to bear a child; the story supports both readings without collapsing into either, which is why it is taught as an exercise in the ethics of consent. Butler's control of tone is the story's real technical achievement: Gan reports the cutting of a man's belly open with the same calm he brings to the smell of the kitchen or the weight of T'Gatoi's limbs, and because he does not tell the reader to be horrified, the horror arrives without interference. The result is a story that can be read as body horror, as a coming-of-age narrative, as a political allegory or as a love story, and that is diminished by any reading which chooses only one of them.
narrative_structure: A single first-person narration in the past tense, covering one night and the following morning; the backstory of the reservation and the Tlic is given in Gan's recollections as they are triggered by the night's events, and the story's climax - the operation - arrives at the centre rather than at the end, so that the decision that follows is the real climax.
meter_and_prosody: Calm, exact, unhurried first-person prose; sensory detail used sparingly and precisely, so that the alien is described in domestic terms; dialogue that carries the political argument without becoming an argument; and a refusal of the horror-genre vocabulary that the material would justify, which is what makes the horror land.
historical_context: First published in Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine, June 1984, and collected in Bloodchild and Other Stories (1995), expanded in 2005. Butler wrote it while preparing for a trip to the Amazon to research the Xenogenesis series, and said that the story began as a way of managing her fear of parasitic insects - the botfly in particular. It won the Hugo and Nebula awards for best novelette in 1985, and the Locus award, and it is the story most often cited in the argument for Butler's place in the canon of American literature.
literary_significance: 'Bloodchild' is Butler's most awarded story and one of the most anthologised American short stories of the 1980s; it is a set text in courses on science fiction, on gender and on the ethics of consent, and its triple award - Hugo, Nebula and Locus - together with its appearance in The Weird and The Big Book of Science Fiction has made it the standard introduction to Butler's shorter work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine, June 1984; collected in Bloodchild and Other Stories (New York: Seven Stories Press, 1995; expanded 2005). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is reproduction and the ownership of the body, which the story literalises by giving the pregnancy to a man and the institution to an alien species. The second is consent: Gan's agreement is not freely given in any simple sense - he has been chosen before he could speak - and yet the story insists that a bargain can be entered into with knowledge and love, and that this is different from being used. The third is the family as the place where the political arrangement is lived: the mother's refusal of the egg, the sister's wish to be chosen, the brother's fear, and Gan's negotiation for their protection all make the reservation a domestic space rather than a metaphor. The fourth is the animal: the Tlic are not villains, and Butler gives them a biology, a politics and an affection that make them legible as persons.
summary: Gan opens the story on 'my last night of childhood', when T'Gatoi, the Tlic official who has been his family's patron since before his birth, brings two sterile eggs - a drug that produces euphoria and protects against the Tlic parasite - and insists that Gan eat one alone. His mother refuses hers, and watches him. Gan's older brother and sisters have already been chosen or passed over; his sister wants to be chosen, and his mother is still coming to terms with the choice that was made for Gan when he was an infant. The night's crisis arrives when another human family, the Lomas, arrive with a man, Bram Lomas, in the final stage of an infestation: a Tlic grub has grown inside him and must be cut out before it kills him, and the operation is performed on the family's kitchen table with the animals of the house watching. Gan, who is expected to watch as part of his education, is horrified, and the horror changes the terms of his consent. In the end he agrees to carry T'Gatoi's children, but on a condition that he negotiates himself - that his own sister and brother be protected and not sold - and the story closes with the two of them together, and with Gan no longer a child.
critical_context: Critics have read the story as an allegory of slavery (a reading Butler resisted), as a thought-experiment about male pregnancy and the ownership of reproductive labour, and as a study in consent and dependency; feminist and queer readings have been central since the 1990s, and the story's refusal to resolve the question of whether the arrangement is exploitation or mutualism is the point on which most criticism turns.
research_notes: The first printing in the June 1984 issue of Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine is recorded from the several published accounts of the story and from the collection's own acknowledgements; the exact page numbers of the magazine printing were not established from the sources consulted.

title: An Agony. As Now.
description: 'An Agony. As Now.' is the sixth poem in The Dead Lecturer (New York: Grove Press, 1964), the collection Baraka published under the name LeRoi Jones a year before the assassination of Malcolm X and two years before he left Greenwich Village for Harlem. It is a first-person poem about being housed in a body that hates the person living in it, and it is the clearest statement in the book of the separation between the poet's public position and his inner life that the whole collection is about.
plot_or_argument: The poem is built on a single conceit - the self as a dwelling occupied by someone else - and it tests that conceit until it yields a political meaning. The 'someone who hates me' is at first a psychological double, the mask the poet wears in the white bohemia of the early 1960s; by the end of the poem it is also the American arrangement in which a Black writer is permitted to be present only as a performance. Baraka's line here is short, flat and unornamented, and the flatness is the point: the poem refuses the lyric consolations that have been available to it and stays with the description of a self divided against itself. The Dead Lecturer is the book in which Baraka breaks with the Beats, and 'An Agony. As Now.' is the poem that states why: the alienation the Beats had made into a style was, for him, not a style but a condition with a history. Read against 'Black Art', written two years later, the poem marks the moment before the turn, when the split could still be recorded as an agony rather than resolved into a programme.
narrative_structure: A single unbroken free-verse lyric of about forty short lines, without stanza divisions in the printed text, moving from the initial statement of enclosure through a middle passage of address to the 'someone' and closing on the body still occupied.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines, hard enjambment and very little metaphor of the ornamental kind; a spoken, almost conversational register interrupted by sudden abstraction; repetition of the pronouns 'I' and 'you' until the two become interchangeable; and a refusal of the cadence that would let the poem close on a consolation.
historical_context: Written in the last years of Baraka's Greenwich Village period and published in The Dead Lecturer (Grove Press, 1964), the collection that marked his break with the Beats and with the white avant-garde. Richard Howard, reviewing the book in The Nation, called the poems 'the agonized poems of a man writing to save his skin'. Within two years of its publication Baraka had left the Village, founded the Black Arts Repertory Theatre/School in Harlem and written 'Black Art'.
literary_significance: 'An Agony. As Now.' is one of the two or three poems by which The Dead Lecturer is known and the standard anthology text for the transition in Baraka's work from Beat-adjacent experiment to Black Arts statement; it is taught as the poem that records the moment before the turn, and it opens the Norton selection of his poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Dead Lecturer (New York: Grove Press, 1964), where it is the sixth poem; collected in Transbluesency: The Selected Poems of Amiri Baraka/LeRoi Jones 1961-1995 (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the divided self, and the poem's peculiar force comes from refusing to allegorise it: the speaker really is inside someone who hates him, and the description is literal before it is symbolic. The second is race as an inner partition, the experience of inhabiting a self that the surrounding society has designed. The third is the failure of love and art as exits: the poem turns towards a woman and towards the city and finds that neither offers a way out of the enclosure. The fourth is the anticipation of the turn Baraka would take - the sense that the agony is a stage to be passed through rather than a condition to be analysed.
summary: The poem begins 'I am inside someone / who hates me.' The speaker looks out through the eyes of that other, watches him eat and drink and move through the world, and describes the humiliation of being carried around by a self that is not his own. The imagery is of enclosure and infection: the body as a room, as a machine, as something the speaker has been put inside rather than something he is. In the middle of the poem the speaker addresses the person he is inside and asks what the arrangement is for; then the poem turns outward, to love, to the woman in the room, to the world of the city, and the private agony becomes a general condition. The poem ends not with resolution but with the speaker still inside, still watching, having discovered that the self he would like to be cannot be reached from where he is standing.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as the psychological hinge of Baraka's career, the point at which the Beat vocabulary of alienation is revealed to have a racial content; the poem's refusal of consolation has been discussed as a formal strategy rather than a failure of resolution, and it is regularly compared with 'Black Dada Nihilismus' from the same volume.
research_notes: The volume, publisher and year are from the library catalogue record of the first edition and its contents list; the poem's position in the volume is from that contents list. The date of composition is not established from the sources consulted, so the record gives the date of first book publication.

title: A Poem for Willie Best
description: 'A Poem for Willie Best' is the longest and most ambitious poem in The Dead Lecturer (Grove Press, 1964). Willie Best was a Black American actor who appeared in more than a hundred Hollywood films from the 1930s to the 1950s, usually as a servant or a comic sidekick, credited for years as 'Sleep 'n' Eat'; Baraka's poem takes the fact of that career - a man paid to perform a caricature of himself - and makes it the model of what American culture does to the Black artist. It is written in numbered sections of varying length and mixes narration, quotation, hallucination and direct address.
plot_or_argument: What makes 'A Poem for Willie Best' the central poem of The Dead Lecturer is that it refuses to let the reader stand outside the machine it describes. Best is not presented as a victim to be pitied but as a worker with a craft, and the poem's anger is directed less at him than at the economy that made his craft into a caricature and at the audience that paid for it. Baraka built the poem out of the materials of American mass culture - the film, the advertisement, the minstrel routine - and set them in a verse that is itself cinematic, cutting between close-up and panorama without transition. The numbered sections keep the poem from settling into a single argument, and the recurring face holds it together as a refrain. The poem's formal risk is its length: Baraka allows the hallucination to run on past the point where a shorter poem would have made its point, so that the reader experiences something of the exhaustion the poem is about. In the last movement the poem turns on its own speaker and asks whether this poem, too, is a performance - which is the question that the whole of Baraka's later work, from 'Black Art' to the Marxist poems, would try to answer, and which none of them would settle. That is why the poem still reads as a threshold rather than a conclusion.
narrative_structure: An extended poem in numbered sections, twenty pages in the first edition, moving between third-person description of Best, hallucinatory catalogue and direct address; the sections vary in length and are not organised by argument, and the poem's coherence is carried by the recurring face and by the speaker's voice.
meter_and_prosody: Long unrhymed free-verse lines that sometimes run to prose; abrupt shifts of register between the demotic and the literary; a montage technique borrowed from film and from jazz; the repetition of a name or phrase as a refrain; and an ending that turns to the second person and raises its voice.
historical_context: Published in The Dead Lecturer (Grove Press, 1964), the collection that marked Baraka's break with the Beats. Willie Best (1916-1962) had died two years before the book appeared, and his career - more than a hundred films, the degrading credit 'Sleep 'n' Eat', a late life of poverty and illness - was recent public knowledge. The poem belongs to the moment just before the Black Arts Movement, when Baraka was working out in verse the argument about the Black artist's relation to the American audience that he would make explicitly in 'The Myth of a Negro Literature' (1962) and in Home: Social Essays (1966).
literary_significance: 'A Poem for Willie Best' is the poem most often cited as the achievement of The Dead Lecturer and as the first full statement of the aesthetic that the Black Arts Movement would adopt; it is widely anthologised, it gave its title to a generation's argument about the Black performer, and criticism treats it as the bridge between Baraka's Beat years and his nationalist work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Dead Lecturer (New York: Grove Press, 1964); collected in Transbluesency (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the manufacture of the Black performer: the poem is a study of how a caricature is produced, cast, paid for and consumed, and it insists on the labour involved rather than the stereotype alone. The second is spectatorship - the audience's share in the arrangement - which is why the poem keeps turning to address the reader. The third is the artist's complicity: Baraka writes about Best while asking what he himself has done for a living, and the question gives the poem its moral pressure. The fourth is the American image-world of the 1950s and early 1960s, the films and advertisements through which a nation learned what a Black face was for. Baraka does not step outside that image-world to judge it; he works inside it, cutting from one piece of it to another, so that the poem reproduces the very condition it is complaining about.
summary: The poem opens with a scene of performance: a face singing alone, a man on a screen doing what he has been hired to do. Baraka describes Best's face, his voice and his routines, and the description keeps sliding from the actor to the audience and back, so that the reader is never sure whether the poem is about the man, the role or the people watching. The middle sections move into a hallucinatory landscape of American images - films, advertisements, lynchings, churches - in which Best's face recurs, and the poem's speaker begins to address him directly, asking what it cost to make the face that the country wanted. The last sections turn to the speaker's own position: the poet who has also been performing, who has also been paid, and who is now trying to write a poem that will not be a performance. The poem ends on an address to the reader - a demand to hear - rather than on an image.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as a study of minstrelsy and its wage, as a precursor of the Black Arts aesthetic, and as an experiment in cinematic form; Adrienne Rich called The Dead Lecturer a book rather than an assemblage of occasional poems, and singled out its 'faultless phrasing', while later criticism has attended to the poem's ambivalence about its own spectatorship.
research_notes: The first edition's contents list gives the poem in the volume; the page extent described above is from the catalogue record of the Grove edition and was not checked against a copy. No printed bibliography of Baraka was consulted.

title: Black Art
description: 'Black Art' was written in 1965, after the assassination of Malcolm X, and first published in The Liberator for January 1966, before being collected in Black Magic (Bobbs-Merrill, 1969). It is the manifesto poem of the Black Arts Movement: a demand that poems be useful, that they be weapons, that they stop describing the world and start changing it, delivered in a voice that alternates between incantation and threat. Its opening - 'Poems are bullshit unless they are / teeth or trees or lemons piled / on a step' - is among the most quoted openings in postwar American poetry.
plot_or_argument: 'Black Art' is a poem that argues against poetry, and its force depends on the contradiction it cannot resolve. Baraka calls for a writing that would stop being writing - that would be action, a bullet, a tree - and he makes the call in an elaborately crafted poem whose rhythms are borrowed from jazz and from the sermon. The poem's obscenity and its anti-Semitic naming have been the centre of its reception: they are inseparable from its historical moment, when the language of Black nationalism was being forged in reaction to the murder of Malcolm X, and they have been the reason it is taught as a document as much as a poem. Baraka himself later repudiated the anti-Semitic strain as a 'reactionary thing' while continuing to defend the poem's central demand. Its formal achievement is the ending, which refuses the lyric turn: there is no image to hold, only a slogan that the poem has spent all its energy making feel like an inevitability. Read beside 'An Agony. As Now.' from two years earlier, it marks the distance Baraka travelled - from a self divided and unable to act to a voice that has decided that the poem is the act, and the shorter distance between that voice and the speaker of the Marxist poems of the 1970s, who would demand the same thing of a different politics.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem of about seventy lines, without stanza divisions in the printed text, built as a series of escalating imperatives and catalogues, with an onomatopoeic passage at the centre and a two-line demand at the end.
meter_and_prosody: Incantatory repetition, hard consonants and a rhythm driven by stress rather than metre; obscenity and racial epithets used as instruments; onomatopoeia and non-semantic sound; a vocabulary drawn from street speech, jazz and the slogan; and an absence of simile, so that the poem's images are asserted as facts.
historical_context: Written in 1965 after the assassination of Malcolm X and first published in The Liberator for January 1966. The poem had already circulated in 1965 as a recorded performance on the drummer Sunny Murray's album Sonny's Time Now, with Albert Ayler, Don Cherry, Lewis Worrell and Henry Grimes, which is why its rhythms sound like the free jazz of the period. Between 1968 and 1973 it was reprinted in more than fifteen anthologies, and it became the founding text of the Black Arts Movement's poetics alongside Larry Neal's essay 'The Black Arts Movement' (1968).
literary_significance: 'Black Art' is the manifesto poem of the Black Arts Movement and one of the most consequential American poems of the 1960s: its opening lines are among the most quoted in postwar poetry, its recorded performance is an early instance of the poem as an audio work, and its demand for a usable art set the terms of the argument about Black aesthetics for a decade.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Liberator, January 1966; collected in Black Magic: Sabotage; Target Study; Black Art (Bobbs-Merrill, 1969) and in Transbluesency (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the function of art: the poem is an ars poetica that defines the poem by what it can do rather than by what it says. The second is violence, both the violence the poem calls for and the violence it answers, which the poem refuses to separate. The third is naming as a political act - the poem's enemies are named in the language of the street rather than analysed, and the naming is itself the argument. The fourth is the Black world the poem wants, which exists in the poem only as a demand, and which the poem's rhythm makes momentarily present. The poem is therefore a document of the moment in which American poetry was asked to choose between craft and use, and it answers by refusing to see the two as alternatives.
summary: The poem begins by clearing the ground: most poems are worthless, and the test of a poem is whether it is a thing in the world - teeth, a tree, lemons on a step - rather than a refinement of feeling. From there it moves into a catalogue of what a Black poem should do: it should be able to kill, it should assassinate, it should 'shoot guns' and 'make our own world'. Baraka names the enemies in the poem's own vocabulary - the 'negroleader', the 'liberal', the 'jewlady', the 'owner-jews' - and the naming is deliberately offensive, part of the poem's argument that a poetry of politeness is a poetry of submission. The middle of the poem turns to sound: 'rrrrrrrrrrrr / tuhtuhtuhtuhtuhtuh', onomatopoeia that turns the poem into the noise of gunfire and of a voice refusing to be grammatical. It ends with a demand rather than an image: 'We want a black poem. And a / Black World.'
critical_context: Criticism treats the poem as the ars poetica of the Black Arts Movement and as the clearest instance of its refusal of the Western lyric; the anti-Semitic passages have been the subject of a substantial literature, including Baraka's own later repudiation, and the poem's relation to the jazz of Albert Ayler and Sunny Murray has been studied as a model of cross-media influence. William J. Harris and Houston Baker read it as the point at which Baraka's modernism becomes a political programme.
research_notes: The Liberator printing of January 1966 and the 1965 recording on Sonny's Time Now are recorded from the sources read, which agree on both; the poem's page extent in Black Magic is not established from the sources consulted.

title: Will They Cry When You're Gone, You Bet
description: 'Will They Cry When You're Gone, You Bet' is a poem of the Black nationalist period, collected in Black Magic: Sabotage; Target Study; Black Art (Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1969), the volume that gathered the poems Baraka wrote between 1961 and 1967. It is an elegy for the dead of the movement and a rebuke to those who survived them, built on a desert landscape in which the speaker's friends lie unburied while the living drift away from them.
plot_or_argument: The poem is Baraka's elegy for the movement's dead, written in the voice of a survivor who has decided that mourning is not enough. Its images are taken from Exodus and from the desert narratives of American preaching - a people in flight, a wilderness, an oasis that recedes - and Baraka turns that inheritance against the liberal culture that, in his account, offers Black Americans a beautiful death instead of a liveable life. The 'white drifting fairies, muses' are the poem's most revealing figure: they are the aesthetic tradition itself, singing in calm tones about transcendence, and the poem's refusal of them is a refusal of the whole idea of a poetry that consoles. The ending is deliberately unresolved - the speaker is still in the desert, the friends are still dead, and the only thing the poem has established is that it will not lie about either fact. It is one of the clearest statements in Black Magic of the position Baraka had reached: that the elegy, like every other form, had to be rebuilt for the use of the living.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem, in one movement, of about sixty lines, built as an address to the survivors that keeps returning to the image of the desert and closes on the refusal of the muses' song.
meter_and_prosody: Long, unpunctuated free-verse lines close to the cadence of a sermon; direct address in the second person plural; a landscape described in flat declaratives; and a vocabulary that mixes the biblical ('oasis', 'muses', 'saints') with the colloquial ('you bet', 'etcetera').
historical_context: Collected in Black Magic: Sabotage; Target Study; Black Art (Bobbs-Merrill, 1969), which gathered the poems of 1961-1967 and which Baraka published at the height of his Black nationalist period, the year of Black Fire (edited with Larry Neal) and of the founding of the Congress of Afrikan People. The poem's dead are those of the movement's first years - the poem is contemporaneous with the elegies for Malcolm X and with the Newark rebellion of 1967.
literary_significance: 'Will They Cry When You're Gone, You Bet' is one of the poems by which the Black Magic volume is known and has been anthologised in the Norton Anthology of American Literature since the 1990s, where it stands beside 'An Agony. As Now.' and 'A Poem for Willie Best' as the third face of Baraka's poetry: the elegiac, public voice of the nationalist years.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Black Magic: Sabotage; Target Study; Black Art (Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1969); reprinted in Transbluesency (1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is mourning under political pressure - the dead of the movement, and the question of what the survivors owe them. The second is desertion, both the literal abandonment of the bodies and the cultural abandonment of the struggle by those who took up the consolations of art. The third is the desert as a figure for America, a place of white heat and no water, which the poem sets against the oasis it refuses to promise. The fourth is the refusal of the muse, which makes the poem an argument about what poetry is for, conducted inside an elegy.
summary: The poem opens with the dead: 'You leave dead friends in a desert.' The speaker addresses those who have walked away from the bodies, describing them as deserted by the living and by themselves, 'leaving themselves, in the foot paths of madmen and saints'. The desert is the poem's central landscape - dry, white, without water - and the people in it are dying of thirst while 'white women serenade them in mystic deviousness', figures of the culture that has distracted them from the struggle. The poem's argument is that the dead are better off than the living who have abandoned them, and that an oasis, even a bitter one, is better than 'white drifting fairies, muses, singing to us, in calm tones, about how it is better to die'. The poem ends by refusing the consolation of art: the muses' song is exactly what the speaker will not accept.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as the elegiac counterpart to 'Black Art' - the same programme, in the mode of mourning rather than demand - and discusses its use of the Exodus narrative and its refusal of the pastoral consolation that the Western elegy traditionally offers; it is also read as evidence of how quickly Baraka's poetry absorbed the deaths of the mid-1960s into a political form.
research_notes: The first printing of the poem in a periodical was not established from the sources consulted; the record therefore gives the date of first book collection, 1969, and does not claim an earlier magazine appearance. The volume and publisher are from the catalogue record of Black Magic.

title: Headwaters
description: 'Headwaters' is the framing poem of The Way to Rainy Mountain (Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press, 1969), Momaday's account of the Kiowa migration from the headwaters of the Yellowstone to the Wichita Mountains. It stands at the front of the book, before the historical introduction and the twenty-four three-part episodes, and sets the terms on which everything after it is read: a people, a migration, a landscape and the act of remembering.
plot_or_argument: 'Headwaters' does the work of a preface in verse: it establishes the geography, the timeframe and the tone of the book that follows, and it does so without explaining anything. Momaday writes the migration as a movement through a landscape whose names are Kiowa, so that the reader learns the country and the history at the same time. The poem's syntax is unhurried and its images are held rather than developed, which is the technique Momaday takes from oral narrative: a thing is named, allowed to stand, and then the poem moves on. The turn at the end - from the ancestors to the speaker - makes the poem a genealogy rather than a travelogue, and it is that turn that licenses the rest of The Way to Rainy Mountain, in which Momaday interleaves Kiowa legend, historical commentary and his own memoir. The poem is short, and its shortness is part of its argument: the origin of a people can be told in a page, if the page is right.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem of about twenty-five lines in four movements: the high country, the descent into the plains, the acquisition of the Kiowa way of life, and the turn to the speaker's present.
meter_and_prosody: Spare free verse with long, balanced sentences and very few adjectives; proper names used without gloss; a rhythm close to spoken narration; and an ending that resolves on a statement of continuance rather than an image.
historical_context: Published as the opening poem of The Way to Rainy Mountain (University of New Mexico Press, 1969), illustrated by the author's father, the Kiowa painter Al Momaday, and written after Momaday had retraced his ancestors' route from Montana to Oklahoma. The book appeared in the year House Made of Dawn won the Pulitzer Prize, and the two together are the founding documents of the Native American Renaissance.
literary_significance: 'Headwaters' is the poem that opens one of the central books of Native American literature and is the standard anthology selection from Momaday's poetry; it appears in the Norton Anthology with the prose selections from the same book, and it is taught as a model of how a poem can carry a people's history.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Way to Rainy Mountain (Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press, 1969), where it opens the volume; reprinted in In the Presence of the Sun: Stories and Poems 1961-1991 (1992). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is origin and migration - the journey from the headwaters to the plains, which is both a historical event and the founding story of the Kiowa as a people. The second is the land as the carrier of memory, since the poem's geography is the argument that the Kiowas' history is locatable. The third is inheritance: the speaker receives the story and becomes its teller, which makes the poem a statement about what a poet does with a tribal past. The fourth is the sacred - the Tai-me and the sun dance - present in the poem without being explained, which is Momaday's way of writing a religious culture without translating it for outsiders.
summary: The poem opens on the high country where the Kiowas began, 'the headwaters of the Yellowstone', and follows them east and south as they come down out of the mountains into the plains, acquiring horses, the sun dance and the Tai-me, and becoming a Plains people. Its images are of descent and arrival: the meadow, the river, the buffalo, the sacred doll. In the closing movement the poem turns from the migration to the present, and to the speaker's own relation to the journey - the story is now his to carry - and the poem ends on a note of continuance rather than loss, with the landscape still holding what the people left in it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as the frame that makes The Way to Rainy Mountain legible, and as an instance of Momaday's 'land ethic' - the proposition that a people's identity is inseparable from the country it moved through; it is usually discussed together with the 'Rainy Mountain Cemetery' poem that closes the book, and with the book's three-voice structure.
research_notes: The bibliographic details are from the record of the University of New Mexico Press edition and from the scholarship on the book, which describes 'Headwaters' as the framing poem that follows the preface and precedes the introduction. The poem was not read in a printed copy for this record.

title: The Way to Rainy Mountain
description: The Way to Rainy Mountain was published by the University of New Mexico Press in 1969, illustrated with eleven drawings by the author's father, the Kiowa painter Al Momaday. It retraces the Kiowa migration from the headwaters of the Yellowstone to the Wichita Mountains of Oklahoma and ends at Rainy Mountain, where Momaday's grandmother Aho lived and is buried. The book is built in three voices on facing pages: a Kiowa legend, a passage of historical commentary, and a fragment of Momaday's own memory, each set in a different typeface.
plot_or_argument: The Way to Rainy Mountain is the book in which Momaday solved the formal problem that Native American writing faced in the 1960s: how to write the history of an oral people without turning their stories into anthropology or into memoir. His answer is the three-voice page, which refuses to subordinate legend to commentary or commentary to memory, and which makes the reader hold all three at once. The effect is cumulative rather than narrative: no single episode explains the migration, but the sequence of them, each with its myth and its fact and its remembered detail, builds a history that is neither the anthropologist's nor the novelist's. The grandmother, Aho, is the book's centre - a woman born in the shadow of the Kiowas' last free years, who told Momaday the stories, and whose death at Rainy Mountain gives the book its destination. The prose is spare and deliberate, with a cadence that Momaday took from Kiowa speech as he had heard it, and the book's most quoted passage, about looking upon the landscape in the early morning 'with the sun at your back', is the clearest statement of its method: the land is not scenery but an instrument of knowledge. It is one of the small number of American books of the period that changed what a book of nonfiction prose could be, and it has been in print continuously since 1969.
narrative_structure: A preface, an introduction, two framing poems and three sections of eight episodes each; every episode is a triptych of legend, commentary and memoir printed in three typefaces on the page, and the book's argument is carried by the arrangement rather than by a continuous narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Restrained, cadenced prose with long periodic sentences and a deliberately archaic formality in the legendary passages; the commentary in a plainer documentary register; the memoir passages in a quieter first person; and an overall design - typeface, illustration, page layout - that is part of the book's meaning.
historical_context: Written after Momaday retraced the Kiowa migration from Montana to Oklahoma in the mid-1960s, and based on an earlier privately printed booklet, The Journey of Tai-me (1967). It was published by the University of New Mexico Press in 1969, the year House Made of Dawn won the Pulitzer Prize, and it is one of the two or three books that opened the Native American Renaissance. Its three-voice form has been widely imitated and is taught as a model of cross-genre writing.
literary_significance: The Way to Rainy Mountain is the central work of Native American nonfiction prose and one of the most influential American books of the period: it has never been out of print, it is a standard text in courses on American autobiography, the essay and Native American literature, and its three-voice form changed the way American writers could put oral tradition on the page.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Albuquerque by the University of New Mexico Press in 1969, with drawings by Al Momaday; based on The Journey of Tai-me (1967); reissued in a twenty-fifth anniversary edition in 1994 and in later editions. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E, which prints the introduction and the episodes IV, XIII, XVII, XXIV and the epilogue.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the migration itself, as event and as the shaping story of a people. The second is the relation of oral tradition to written history: the book puts the two side by side, in different typefaces, and refuses to arbitrate between them. The third is the grandmother and the family - Aho, the Tai-me keeper's descendant, and Momaday's own childhood among the Kiowa and Jemez - through whom the abstract history becomes personal. The fourth is dispossession and survival: the surrender at Fort Sill, the confinement to the reservation near Rainy Mountain, and the continuity of the stories afterwards. The fifth is the landscape as a site of knowledge, an idea the book states in its most famous passage and enacts on every page.
summary: The book opens with a preface and an introduction, framed by two poems, 'Headwaters' and 'Rainy Mountain Cemetery', and then divides into three sections - 'The Setting Out', 'The Going On' and 'The Closing In' - each containing eight episodes. Every episode is a triptych: on the left-hand page a Kiowa myth or story, in the words of the oral tradition; on the right, a paragraph of historical and anthropological commentary on the same subject; and below it, in italic, a passage of Momaday's own recollection, usually of his childhood at Jemez or of his grandmother. The episodes trace the migration, the acquisition of the horse and the sun dance, the Tai-me, the wars with the United States, the surrender at Fort Sill in 1875 and the settlement near Rainy Mountain. The book closes with the grandmother's death and with the poem 'Rainy Mountain Cemetery', and with Momaday's account of returning to the mountain.
critical_context: Criticism has read the book as the founding example of 'tribal autobiography', as a critique of anthropological appropriation, and as a formal experiment in the juxtaposition of oral and written history; the typeface and layout have been discussed as constitutive of its meaning rather than decorative, and the book's relation to The Journey of Tai-me (1967) has been studied as an instance of a writer revising his own materials.
research_notes: The book's structure, illustrations and publisher are recorded from the bibliographic and scholarly sources read, not from a copy of the first edition. The Norton selection is an excerpt, recorded here as one work with its parts named in the bibliography statement.

title: The Summer Day
description: 'The Summer Day' was first published in House of Light (Boston: Beacon Press, 1990) and is the most quoted American poem of the last thirty years. It begins with a question about who made the world, passes through the observation of a grasshopper, and ends with a question addressed to the reader about what they intend to do with their life. It is a poem of attention that turns, in its last line, into a demand.
plot_or_argument: 'The Summer Day' is a poem about attention, and it earns its famous ending by refusing to hurry towards it. The first half is almost entirely questions and observation: the grasshopper is described with a naturalist's precision - the jaws, the eyes, the sugar - and the speaker does not interpret it. The turn comes with the word 'prayer', which the poem introduces tentatively, as something the speaker cannot define but can enact through attention. From there the poem moves outward into the fields, into idleness, into the idea of being 'blessed', and the movement is deliberately undramatic: nothing happens except that the speaker spends a day looking. The ending's power comes from the shift of address. For thirteen lines the poem has been spoken to no one, and in the last four it turns on the reader and asks a question that the rest of the poem has been quietly making possible - if attention is all we have, what are you doing with your life? The poem's simplicity is its risk and its achievement: Oliver's critics have called it prose with line breaks, and her readers have taken it as a credo, which is a fate few poems of the period have had. The question is unanswerable inside the poem, and the poem knows it: it offers no model of a good life, only the demand that the reader notice the one they are already living.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse lyric of nineteen lines in one stanza, unrhymed, moving from question to observation to reflection to a closing address, with no section breaks and an ending that turns from the first person to the second, so that the poem's last movement is also its only moment of direct speech.
meter_and_prosody: Short free-verse lines with heavy enjambment; almost no metaphor, and where figures appear they are homely ('fall down into the grass'); a conversational register carried by rhetorical questions; and a closing quatrain of direct address that is deliberately plain.
historical_context: Published in House of Light (Beacon Press, 1990), the collection that won the Christopher Award and the L. L. Winship/PEN New England Award, and reprinted in New and Selected Poems (1992). By 1990 Oliver was the best-selling poet in the United States, and 'The Summer Day' became - through readings, quotations and its use in commencement addresses and in the 'grasshopper' name by which many readers know it - the most widely circulated American poem of its period.
literary_significance: 'The Summer Day' is the most quoted American poem of the last three decades and the one most often used to introduce readers to poetry; its closing question is part of the common American vocabulary, and it is a set text in schools and in courses on nature writing. Its critical reception is a case study in the relation between a poet's popular readership and the academy.
bibliographical_notes: First published in House of Light (Boston: Beacon Press, 1990); reprinted in New and Selected Poems (1992) and The Truro Bear and Other Adventures (2008). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is attention as a form of prayer, stated explicitly in the poem's middle lines and enacted in its first half. The second is the particularity of the natural world: the grasshopper is not a symbol but a creature with jaws and eyes, and the poem's insistence on that is what keeps it from being a greeting card. The third is mortality, raised in the penultimate question and left to stand. The fourth is the reader, who is addressed directly at the end and made responsible for the poem's question, which is why the poem is so often quoted out of context as an injunction.
summary: The poem opens with four questions: 'Who made the world? / Who made the swan, and the black bear? / Who made the grasshopper?' The speaker then describes the grasshopper - this one, in the grass, not the species - eating sugar out of her hand, moving her jaws back and forth 'instead of up and down', and looking around 'with her enormous and complicated eyes'. The poem then widens: the speaker says she does not know exactly what a prayer is, but she knows how to pay attention, how to fall down into the grass, how to be idle and blessed, and how to walk through the fields, which is what she has been doing all day. The last lines turn to the reader: 'Tell me, what else should I have done? / Doesn't everything die at last, and too soon? / Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?'
critical_context: Critics divide over the poem: some read it as a genuine devotional lyric in the tradition of Whitman and Hopkins, others as a sentimental simplification of that tradition, and the argument has become a standard topic in discussions of American poetry's public. Its formal plainness has been defended as a deliberate poetics of attention and attacked as prose arranged on the page; feminist and ecocritical readings have emphasised the poem's refusal of mastery over the natural world it describes.
research_notes: The first printing in House of Light is recorded from the publisher's own note on the poem and from the Poetry Foundation's page; no earlier periodical appearance was established, and the record therefore dates the poem 1990.

title: miss rosie
description: 'miss rosie' was published in Lucille Clifton's first collection, Good Times (New York: Random House, 1969). It is a portrait of an old woman the speaker has known since childhood, seen now sitting with her bag among the garbage cans of an American city, and it is the poem that established the voice - lower case, unpunctuated, plain, unsparing and tender at once - that Clifton would use for the rest of her life.
plot_or_argument: 'miss rosie' is a poem of twenty short lines that does the work of a short story, and its economy is the point: Clifton gives the woman's whole history in a phrase - 'the best looking gal in town' - and her present in three details: the coat, the bag, the corner. The poem's grammar is doing something careful. The speaker 'watches' miss rosie, which is the position of a spectator, and then refuses that position by standing up; the final lines collapse the distance between the two women, so that the poem becomes an act of identification rather than of observation. That movement - from seeing to standing with - is the ethical core of Clifton's early work, and it is why the poem is taught as an example of a portrait that refuses to sentimentalise the person it honours. The lower-case spelling and the absence of punctuation, which Clifton adopted from the start, give the poem the sound of a voice speaking rather than a text being read, and the line breaks fall where a breath would.
narrative_structure: One short free-verse poem of about twenty lines, unpunctuated and in lower case, addressed in the second person to miss rosie and closing with a first-person declaration.
meter_and_prosody: Lower case throughout, no punctuation, line breaks at the breath; a plain vocabulary with a few startling phrases ('through your destruction'); repetition of the word 'watched' as a refrain; and an ending that is a short declarative sentence.
historical_context: Published in Good Times (Random House, 1969), Clifton's first collection, which The New York Times named one of the ten best books of the year. The book appeared at the end of the decade in which the civil rights movement had turned to the urban North, and its portraits of Buffalo and of people like miss rosie belong to that moment. It is the earliest poem in the Norton selection of Clifton's work.
literary_significance: 'miss rosie' is one of the two or three poems by which Clifton is best known and the standard introduction to her work; it is anthologised throughout American school and university literature, and it established the portrait poem of urban Black life that she would return to for forty years.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Good Times (New York: Random House, 1969); collected in Good Woman: Poems and a Memoir 1969-1980 (1987) and The Collected Poems of Lucille Clifton 1965-2010 (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the destruction that poverty and age work on a person, recorded without euphemism. The second is the gaze: the poem is about who is looked at and who is looking, and its ethical turn is the speaker's refusal to remain a spectator. The third is the city - the corner, the garbage cans, the bag - as the place where such lives are lived and seen. The fourth is solidarity, stated in the last line as a fact of the speaker's own standing, which is also the poem's tacit claim about what a poem can do.
summary: The poem addresses miss rosie directly and describes her: a woman who was once 'the best looking gal in town', now wrapped in an old coat, sitting 'through your destruction' with her bag beside her. The speaker says she has watched miss rosie for years - 'I have watched you / through your destruction / I have stood on the corner and watched you' - and then makes the declaration on which the poem turns: 'through your destruction / i stand up'. The poem ends with the speaker asserting that she is the same as miss rosie, or that she stands in the same place, and that the old woman's survival is her own.
critical_context: Critics read the poem as a study in the ethics of the gaze and as an early instance of Clifton's identification with the marginalised figures of her childhood; it is usually discussed with 'the lost baby poem' and 'homage to my hips' as the three faces of her early work - witness, grief and celebration.
research_notes: The 1969 first publication in Good Times is recorded from the EBSCO and Poetry for Students accounts and from the collection's contents; the poem was not read in a copy of the first edition.

title: the lost baby poem
description: 'the lost baby poem' was published in Good News About the Earth (New York: Random House, 1972), Clifton's second collection. It is an elegy for a pregnancy that was ended, spoken by a woman who is also the mother of living children, and it moves through guilt, address and a final blessing without ever settling into a single attitude towards what happened.
plot_or_argument: 'the lost baby poem' is the most discussed of Clifton's early poems because it refuses every position its subject offers. It is not a poem of simple grief, because the speaker explains the decision and does not repent it; it is not a poem of justification, because the guilt is present in every line; and it is not a religious poem in any settled sense, although it ends by committing the child to the rivers and the sea in a gesture that borrows the language of baptism. Clifton's technique here is the one she would use for forty years: short unpunctuated lines, a plain vocabulary, a repeated word or phrase to hold the poem together, and an ending that is a single flat sentence carrying an enormous weight. The water imagery, which the EBSCO reading traces from sewage through ice to the rivers of the last stanza, is the poem's structural device: the child moves through it from pollution to consecration, and the reader is carried along by the imagery rather than argued into a judgement. It is a poem about poverty as much as about loss - the decision is presented as an economic one - and that is why it has been central to the feminist and Black feminist reading of Clifton's work. The poem has also been read as an elegy that refuses the elegy's consolations, since its committal of the child to the rivers is a letting-go rather than a promise of reunion, and that refusal is what keeps it from being a poem about forgiveness.
narrative_structure: A free-verse elegy in three stanzas, unpunctuated and in lower case, addressed to the lost child, moving from the circumstances of the loss through a conditional promise to a final committal; the lines are short enough that the poem reads as a single held breath, and the three stanzas mark the only structural division Clifton allows.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines in lower case; a plain and often monosyllabic vocabulary; repetition of the water imagery through the three stanzas; and an ending that resolves into a single declarative sentence.
historical_context: Published in Good News About the Earth (Random House, 1972), the collection that followed Good Times and that also contains Clifton's poems on the Kent State shootings and her sequence on Biblical figures. The poem belongs to the early 1970s, when Black feminist writing was beginning to make the conditions of Black motherhood a public literary subject, and it has become a standard text in that discussion.
literary_significance: 'the lost baby poem' is among the most anthologised and most discussed American poems of the period on abortion and motherhood; it is a set text in courses on American poetry, on Black women's writing and on feminist literature, and it is usually taken as the poem in which Clifton's characteristic voice fully arrives.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Good News About the Earth (New York: Random House, 1972); collected in Good Woman (1987) and The Collected Poems (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is abortion, treated without either the pro-life or the pro-choice vocabulary of the period: the poem's terms are the winter, the money, the other children, and the decision is a fact to be mourned rather than a position to be defended. The second is poverty as a condition of motherhood, which the poem states plainly and without indignation. The third is the religious imagination - the water, the blessing, the committal - which the poem uses without adopting a doctrine. The fourth is address: the poem speaks to the child, which makes it an elegy that cannot be sure it has the right to mourn, and that uncertainty is its emotional engine.
summary: The poem begins with the 'almost body' that was lost and with the speaker's account of the circumstances: the winter, the poverty, the other children who needed what there was. She addresses the lost child directly and imagines it in the water - the sewage, the sea, the ice - and the imagery moves from pollution to baptism as the poem proceeds. In the middle the speaker makes a promise: if she had let the child be born, she says, she would have done certain things, or would not have; the grammar of the promise is deliberately tangled, since the child was not born and the promise can only be conditional. The poem ends by committing the child to the care of something larger than the speaker - the rivers, the sea, the natural world that the poem has been moving towards - and by asking forgiveness, or granting it.
critical_context: Feminist and Black feminist criticism has read the poem as a refusal of the sentimental motherhood of the era and as an insistence on the material conditions of reproductive choice; formal criticism has attended to its unpunctuated syntax and to the water imagery that carries the poem from pollution to blessing, and the poem's relation to the elegy has been widely discussed.
research_notes: The 1972 first publication is recorded from the EBSCO Research Starters entry, which gives the collection and the year, and from the University of Arizona's Voca catalogue citation of the Random House edition; the poem was not read in a copy of the first edition.

title: homage to my hips
description: 'homage to my hips' was published in Two-Headed Woman (Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press, 1980), which won the Juniper Prize. It is a short poem of celebration in which the speaker's hips are described as big, free, mighty and magic, and it is among the most anthologised American poems of the period - a body poem that is also a poem about Black women's refusal of the shapes the culture has prescribed for them.
plot_or_argument: 'homage to my hips' works by taking a part of the body that the culture has made into an object of shame or fetish and making it the subject of a declaration. The poem is funny, and the humour is part of its politics: 'they don't fit into little pretty places' is a joke about small chairs and a statement about a whole aesthetic. Clifton's formal decision is to keep the poem short and the lines almost identical in length, so that the repetition accumulates force rather than variety. The word 'enslaved' in the middle of the poem is the hinge: it moves the poem from body pride to history, and it claims for the speaker's body a lineage of resistance rather than of victimhood. The ending's 'magic' is not a retreat into fantasy but a claim on the power the poem has spent its lines establishing, and it is why the poem reads as a blessing rather than a boast.
narrative_structure: A single short free-verse poem of about twenty lines, unpunctuated and in lower case, built as a series of parallel assertions with 'hips' recurring as a refrain, and closing on a two-line declaration.
meter_and_prosody: Lower case, no punctuation, very short lines; a plain vocabulary and a syntax close to speech; anaphora and refrain; and a tone that moves between comedy and celebration without breaking.
historical_context: Published in Two-Headed Woman (Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press, 1980), which won the Juniper Prize and which is divided into three sequences, 'homage to mine', 'two-headed woman' and 'the light that came to lucille clifton'. The poem belongs to the flourishing of Black feminist writing at the end of the 1970s, alongside the work of Audre Lorde and Toni Cade Bambara, and it has become one of the most quoted American poems on the body.
literary_significance: 'homage to my hips' is the most widely circulated of Clifton's poems after 'miss rosie' and the one most often taught as an example of Black feminist body poetics; it is anthologised in school and university texts and in collections of American poetry, and it has become a fixture of readings and of the public performance of her work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Two-Headed Woman (Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press, 1980); collected in Good Woman (1987), Blessing the Boats (2000) and The Collected Poems (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the female body as a site of both social discipline and self-possession. The second is race: the poem's speaker is a Black woman, the body described is the one the culture has caricatured, and the word 'enslaved' makes the connection explicit. The third is speech itself - the lower case, the repetition, the chant - which the poem uses to make a claim that would sound merely assertive in a different register. The fourth is joy, which the poem treats as a political achievement rather than a private mood.
summary: The poem begins 'these hips are big hips' and proceeds by a series of assertions: they need space, they do not fit into 'little pretty places', they are free, they have never been enslaved, they go where they want to go. In the second movement the speaker says she has known them to 'put a spell on a man and / spin him like a top', and the poem ends with the hips declared mighty and magic. The vocabulary is deliberately simple and the repetition of 'hips' at the end of each line gives the poem the structure of a chant.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a Black feminist reclamation of the body and as an instance of Clifton's use of the chant and the refrain; it is frequently discussed alongside Lorde's 'Uses of the Erotic' and with the body poems of the 1970s, and its humour has been read as a deliberate strategy for making a political claim without adopting a political register.
research_notes: The collection, publisher and prize are recorded from the catalogue and reference records read; the poem's place in the volume's first sequence is from the collection's contents as recorded by those sources.

title: wishes for sons
description: 'wishes for sons' was published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (Brockport, New York: BOA Editions, 1991). It is a poem of comic revenge in which a mother wishes on her sons the physical indignities of menstruation and menopause, so that they might know what women's bodies endure, and it is one of the most quoted poems in Clifton's later work.
plot_or_argument: 'wishes for sons' is a curse poem, and its comedy is exact. Clifton takes the register of the maternal blessing - the thing a mother is supposed to give a son - and fills it with the physiological facts that sons are not supposed to know about their mothers and sisters. The list structure is the poem's engine: each wish is a small, specific humiliation, and the accumulation of them turns the poem from a joke into an argument about whose experience counts as real. The final turn to the gynecologists is the sharpest move in the poem, because it shifts the target from the sons' ignorance to the institutions that share it. Clifton's line here is almost entirely without metaphor - the poem is a list of things that happen to bodies - and the flatness is what makes the last line land. It is a poem that has been read as merely funny and as a precise piece of feminist argument, and it is both.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem of about twenty lines, unpunctuated and in lower case, built as a list of wishes in two movements - the menstrual and the menopausal - and closing on a single line about the gynecologists.
meter_and_prosody: Lower case, no punctuation, very short lines; a plain and bodily vocabulary ('cramps', 'tampon', 'clots', 'hot flashes'); a list structure carried by anaphora ('i wish them'); and a tone that is comic on the surface and entirely serious underneath.
historical_context: Published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991), the volume in which Clifton arranged her poems of the late 1980s in four sequences named after quilt patterns. The poem belongs to the period of her widest recognition as a feminist poet, after the death of her husband in 1984 and alongside The Book of Light (1993).
literary_significance: 'wishes for sons' is one of the most widely quoted poems in Clifton's later work and a standard anthology piece in courses on American poetry and on women's writing; its closing line is among the most cited in her work, and it is regularly read as a compact statement of the feminist argument about embodied knowledge.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (Brockport, NY: BOA Editions, 1991); collected in Blessing the Boats (2000) and The Collected Poems (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the asymmetry of bodily knowledge between men and women, stated as a list of things sons do not know. The second is the maternal voice turned against its own convention: the blessing becomes a curse that is also a lesson. The third is the medical profession, which the last line makes the poem's real addressee. The fourth is time, since the poem moves from menstruation to menopause and asks the sons to age as women age, which is the poem's most serious wish.
summary: The poem begins 'i wish them cramps' and proceeds through a list of wishes: a strange town, the last tampon, no 7-11, one week early in a white skirt, one week late. The second movement moves forward in time to menopause - hot flashes, clots 'like you wouldn't believe' - and asks that the flashes come when they meet someone special and the clots when they want to. The poem ends with the wish that they be brought to 'gynecologists / not unlike themselves', which is the poem's joke and its judgement: the sons will meet the medical profession as women meet it, and will be understood by men who resemble them.
critical_context: Feminist criticism reads the poem as a comic inversion of the maternal blessing and as an argument about the epistemology of the body; it is usually discussed with 'to my last period' and 'poem to my uterus' as Clifton's sequence on the female body across a lifetime, and its humour has been analysed as a mode of political statement.
research_notes: The first publication in Quilting is recorded from the contents lists of the volume and of the collected poems; the poem was not read in a copy of the first edition.

title: blessing the boats
description: 'blessing the boats' was published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991), where it gives its name to the last of the volume's four sequences, and it later became the title poem of Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems 1988-2000 (2000), which won the National Book Award. It is a poem of farewell and safe passage, addressed to someone setting out on water, and it is one of the most quoted American blessings of the period.
plot_or_argument: 'blessing the boats' is a poem built entirely of subjunctive wishes, and its power comes from the fact that it asks for almost nothing except safe passage. Clifton's images are drawn from the sea - the tide, the wind, the water - and they are handled without ornament: the tide 'entering the lip of our understanding' is the poem's one elaborate figure, and after it the wishes become plainer and shorter, as though the poem were learning to speak.
