The word 'innocence' near the end is the most surprising in the poem, since Clifton's work is rarely innocent about anything; here it names the condition of the person setting out, who does not know what the water holds. The final phrase, 'sail through this to that', is the poem's achievement: it declines to name either shore, so that the blessing can be said over any crossing, and it does so in four monosyllables. It is a religious poem without a doctrine and a love poem without a beloved, and that is why it has become one of the most used poems in American public life.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem of about eighteen very short lines, unpunctuated and in lower case, built as a sequence of 'may' clauses addressed to a departing 'you', and closing on a four-word phrase.
meter_and_prosody: Extremely short lines and minimal punctuation; a vocabulary of sea and weather used plainly; anaphora on 'may'; and an ending that reduces to monosyllables.
historical_context: Published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991) and used as the title poem of Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems 1988-2000 (2000), which won the National Book Award in 2000. The poem was read at Clifton's public appearances throughout the last decade of her life and has become a standard text at memorial services, which is a fate the poem's own refusal to specify its crossing made possible.
literary_significance: 'blessing the boats' is the poem that gave its title to the collection that won Clifton the National Book Award, and it is one of the most widely used American poems of the period at public occasions; it is a standard anthology selection and the poem most often chosen to represent Clifton's late manner.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (Brockport, NY: BOA Editions, 1991); the title poem of Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems 1988-2000 (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 2000). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is passage - the crossing from one condition to another, left unspecified so that it can be a journey, a life or a death. The second is fear, which the poem names once and then moves past, since the blessing is designed to carry the traveller out beyond 'the face of fear'. The third is innocence as a condition of setting out, which the poem values without admiring. The fourth is the water itself, which Clifton uses as her standing figure for what cannot be controlled and what can nonetheless be blessed.
summary: The poem consists of a series of wishes for a voyage: 'may the tide / that is entering even now / the lip of our understanding / carry you out / beyond the face of fear'; may you kiss the wind and turn from it, certain that it will love your back; may you open your eyes to water, 'water waving forever'; and may you, 'in your innocence', sail through 'this to that'. The address is to a 'you' who is departing, and the poem never specifies whether the voyage is a journey, a death or a life; the ambiguity is deliberate and is what makes the poem usable at weddings, funerals and readings of every kind.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a secular blessing and as an instance of Clifton's late style, in which the short line and the subjunctive carry the whole weight; it is discussed with the poems of The Book of Light and The Terrible Stories as the mature form of the religious imagination that runs through her work from Good News About the Earth onwards.
research_notes: The first publication in Quilting is recorded from the volume's contents lists; the National Book Award for Blessing the Boats is from the award records. The poem was not read in a copy of the first edition.

title: to my last period
description: 'to my last period' was published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991). It addresses the speaker's final menstrual period as 'girl', a companion of thirty-eight years who is now leaving, and it turns the end of fertility into a poem of friendship, irritation and farewell.
plot_or_argument: 'to my last period' is a poem about an ending that the culture has no good language for, and Clifton's solution is to treat the ending as a relationship. The address to 'girl' does the work: it makes the period a person with a long history, and it lets the speaker be ambivalent without being either ungrateful or sentimental. The 'red dress' is the poem's one flourish, and it is a good one, since it turns the menstrual blood into a garment and the arrival into a social occasion. What follows is deliberately flat - 'without trouble for me / somewhere, somehow' - and the flatness is the point, since the poem is refusing the lyric intensities that the subject invites. The ending's even tone is the hardest thing in the poem to achieve, and it is what makes the poem usable: it gives a reader a way of saying goodbye to a bodily era without having to choose between mourning and relief. It is one of the poems that has made Clifton central to the feminist writing of the body in the 1980s and 1990s.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem of about fourteen lines, unpunctuated and in lower case, addressed in the second person to the period and framed as a goodbye.
meter_and_prosody: Lower case, minimal punctuation, very short lines; a conversational register with one striking image ('splendid in your red dress'); and an ending that refuses emphasis.
historical_context: Published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991); Clifton was in her early fifties when the poems of the volume were written, and the collection's sequences move through the body, family and history. The poem belongs with 'wishes for sons' and 'poem to my uterus' to a group of poems on menstruation and menopause that were unusual in American poetry of the period for their frankness and their lack of either shame or triumph.
literary_significance: 'to my last period' is one of the most quoted poems in Clifton's later work and a standard anthology selection on the body and ageing; it is regularly cited as an example of how her plain style can carry a subject that American poetry had largely avoided.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (Brockport, NY: BOA Editions, 1991); collected in Blessing the Boats (2000) and The Collected Poems (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the end of fertility, treated as a relationship ending rather than as a loss of function. The second is time, counted in the poem's 'thirty-eight years' and felt in the difference between the opening 'goodbye' and the poem's even tone. The third is the body's ordinary trouble, which the poem records without dramatising. The fourth is the refusal of the available narratives - the medical, the nostalgic and the liberatory - which the poem acknowledges and declines.
summary: The poem opens 'well, girl, goodbye, / after thirty-eight years', and establishes at once the intimacy of the address: the period is a girl, an old companion, someone the speaker has lived with for nearly four decades. The speaker recalls that she 'never arrived / splendid in your red dress / without trouble for me / somewhere, somehow', which is both a complaint and an affectionate one. The poem then turns to the present and to what the ending means, and it refuses both the cultural narrative of loss and the counter-narrative of liberation. It ends with a goodbye that is neither relieved nor grieving, and the evenness of tone is the poem's achievement.
critical_context: Feminist criticism reads the poem as a reclamation of menopause from the medical and cultural narratives that frame it as decline; formal criticism attends to the address and to the deliberate flatness of the ending, and the poem is usually discussed with 'wishes for sons' as the comic and the elegiac faces of the same subject.
research_notes: The first publication in Quilting is recorded from the contents lists of the volume; the poem was not read in a copy of the first edition.

title: wild blessings
description: 'wild blessings' was published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991), in the volume's first sequence. It is a short poem of thanks for the ungovernable parts of a life - the wild, the unasked-for, the things that arrive without being sent for - and it is one of the clearest statements of the religious imagination that runs through Clifton's later work.
plot_or_argument: 'wild blessings' is a poem of gratitude that refuses to be pious. Clifton's subject is the difference between the life one plans and the life one gets, and her formal choice is to make the poem a list rather than an argument, so that the reader receives the blessings in the same unordered way the speaker did. The word 'wild' is doing a lot of work: it names what is not domesticated, not chosen and not controlled, and it associates the sacred with the unmanageable rather than with the orderly. That association is characteristic of Clifton's late work, in which God is more often found in the ungovernable than in the institution. The poem's shortness is part of its meaning: a blessing is not an essay, and Clifton's decision to let the poem be as brief as a grace note is what keeps it from becoming a sermon. It is a useful companion to 'blessing the boats', which makes the same move with a voyage rather than a life.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem, unpunctuated and in lower case, built as a list of thanks with a closing acceptance; about a dozen lines.
meter_and_prosody: Lower case, minimal punctuation, short lines; a plain vocabulary with a few words of weather and growth; and an incantatory repetition of the gesture of thanks.
historical_context: Published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (BOA Editions, 1991), whose four sequences are named after quilt patterns and which gathers Clifton's poems of the late 1980s, a period that followed the death of her husband and in which her work turned increasingly towards blessing and elegy.
literary_significance: 'wild blessings' is one of the poems by which the late manner of Clifton's work is known, and it is anthologised as an example of her religious writing; it is less widely quoted than 'blessing the boats' but belongs to the same group, and it is used in courses on American poetry and on spirituality in literature.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Quilting: Poems 1987-1990 (Brockport, NY: BOA Editions, 1991); collected in Blessing the Boats (2000) and The Collected Poems (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is gratitude for what was not asked for, which the poem treats as the shape of a real life. The second is the sacred, located in the wild rather than the institutional. The third is the refusal of control - the poem does not ask for the wild things to be tamed, and its acceptance is its ethics. The fourth is memory, since the blessings are recollected rather than anticipated, which gives the poem its backward look.
summary: The poem gives thanks for what has not been planned: for the 'wild' blessings that come unbidden, for the parts of a life that were not arranged by the self. Its images are of weather, growth and animals, and its grammar is that of the blessing or the grace before a meal - a list of what is being thanked for, offered without explanation. The poem closes by accepting the wildness rather than trying to bring it under control, and the acceptance is the poem's argument.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an instance of Clifton's theology of the ungovernable, and discusses it with the blessings and thanksgivings of Blessing the Boats and Mercy; the poem's brevity has been read as a formal expression of the grace-note rather than as a limitation.
research_notes: The volume attribution and sequence are from the contents lists of Quilting and of the collected poems; the poem was not read in a copy of the first edition for this record.

title: Poetry Is Not a Luxury
description: 'Poetry Is Not a Luxury' was first published in Chrysalis: A Magazine of Women's Culture in 1977 and collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (Trumansburg, New York: The Crossing Press, 1984). It is Lorde's statement of a poetics: poetry, she argues, is not an ornament added to political struggle but the means by which women - and Black women in particular - discover what they know, and therefore the precondition of any action they might take.
plot_or_argument: 'Poetry Is Not a Luxury' is a short essay that does the work of a manifesto, and its argument is more exact than its title suggests. Lorde is not claiming that poetry is pleasant or useful; she is claiming that it is epistemological - that the poem is the instrument by which a feeling is converted into a thought, and that without that conversion the thought cannot be acted on. The essay's political force comes from its insistence that this is especially true for Black women, whose knowledge has been systematically refused a form. The 'Black mother' passage, which is also a passage about her own mother, gives the argument its ground: the daughters have to learn to recognise their own feeling as knowledge, and the poems that do that are not luxuries but the first acts of a politics. The essay's rhetoric is deliberately plain and its sentences are short, and its closing claim - that poetry 'is not a luxury' but 'a vital necessity of our existence' - has become one of the most quoted sentences in twentieth-century feminist criticism.
narrative_structure: A short prose essay of about fifteen hundred words in five or six unnumbered sections, moving from the definition of poetry, through the argument about feeling and thought, to the Black mother passage, to a closing statement about change.
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative sentences with occasional incantatory repetition; a first-person plural that includes the reader; a vocabulary drawn from both the poetic and the political; and a closing that raises the register without becoming rhetorical.
historical_context: First published in Chrysalis: A Magazine of Women's Culture in 1977 and collected in Sister Outsider (1984). It belongs to the flourishing of Black feminist theory at the end of the 1970s and is a companion piece to 'Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power' (1978), delivered as a paper at the Fourth Berkshire Conference on the History of Women in 1978 and published the same year.
literary_significance: 'Poetry Is Not a Luxury' is one of the founding texts of Black feminist criticism and among the most cited essays in twentieth-century American letters; it is a set text in courses on feminist theory, on poetics and on African American literature, and its title has become a common phrase in discussions of art and politics.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Chrysalis: A Magazine of Women's Culture, no. 1 (1977); collected in Sister Outsider: Essays and Speeches (Trumansburg, NY: The Crossing Press, 1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is poetry as a mode of knowledge rather than a decoration, which the essay argues by locating thought in feeling. The second is the refusal of the language women have been given, and the work of naming what has been 'nameless'. The third is race and gender together: the essay's argument is made for women in general and for Black women in particular, and it refuses to separate the two. The fourth is the future, which the essay treats as something the poem makes possible rather than merely imagines.
summary: The essay begins from the distinction between poetry as 'the way we help give name to the nameless so it can be thought' and the 'luxury' of the title, which is a word Lorde takes from the culture's own condescension towards art and turns against it. She argues that for women the poem is not a refinement but a necessity, because the feelings that precede thought have to be given form before they can become ideas, and because the language available to women has been made by others. The middle of the essay turns on the 'Black mother' and on the daughters who must learn to hear their own knowledge, and it insists on the difference between the 'yes' that is a genuine assent and the 'yes' that is compliance. It closes with the claim that poetry lays 'the foundations for a future of change' and that it is the task of women to make it.
critical_context: Criticism treats the essay as a foundational statement of Black feminist poetics, and reads its argument about feeling and thought alongside Lorde's 'Uses of the Erotic' and the essays of Sister Outsider; it has been central to the theorisation of what is now called 'poethics' and to discussions of the relation between aesthetics and political practice.
research_notes: The Chrysalis first printing of 1977 and the collection in Sister Outsider (1984) are recorded from the sources read; the number of the Chrysalis issue was not established from those sources.

title: Footnote to Howl
description: 'Footnote to Howl' closes Howl and Other Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1956), the collection that made Ginsberg the central poet of the Beat Generation and that was the subject of the 1957 obscenity trial in San Francisco. It is a litany of the word 'holy' - fifteen lines of it, applied to everything the culture had declared unholy - and it is the poem in which Ginsberg's prophetic voice is fully established.
plot_or_argument: 'Footnote to Howl' is a poem of pure assertion, and its form is the oldest one available: the litany. Ginsberg takes the word that the religious tradition reserves for the sacred and applies it to the body, and the repetition is the argument - by the time the reader reaches the fourth 'holy the', the distinction between the sacred and the obscene has been destroyed by accumulation rather than by reasoning. The poem's openness to everything is its politics: in 1956, when the book was published by City Lights and seized by the customs, a list that includes 'holy the cock and holy the cunt' alongside 'holy the grandmother' was an act of defiance. The final fourfold refrain is a formal decision - the litany is not closed with a statement but with a repetition, so that the poem does not so much end as stop, which keeps its assertion from becoming a conclusion. Read as the last part of Howl, it answers the despair of the poem's opening: if all is holy, then 'Moloch' is included too, and the prophetic denunciation becomes a universal affirmation. The litany has been imitated ever since, by poets and by preachers, and it is the source of the poem's continuing life in performance: it is almost impossible to read aloud without beginning to chant.
narrative_structure: A single litany of fifteen long lines in free verse, unrhymed, every line beginning with 'Holy', followed by a four-line coda of 'Holy holy holy holy'.
meter_and_prosody: Long free-verse lines with extensive parallelism and anaphora; capitalization used emphatically; a vocabulary that mixes the liturgical with the obscene; and an incantatory repetition designed for oral delivery, since Ginsberg composed the poem for the reading room rather than the page and its effect depends on the accumulation of the word in the ear.
historical_context: Published as the closing poem of Howl and Other Poems (City Lights Books, 1956), in a first run of four thousand copies and in the 'Pocket Poets' series; copies were seized by the US Customs Service in 1957 and the publisher Lawrence Ferlinghetti was tried for obscenity in San Francisco, and the acquittal that followed became a landmark in post-war American free expression. The poem was written in Berkeley in the summer of 1955, in the burst of composition that also produced 'Howl' and 'A Supermarket in California'.
literary_significance: 'Footnote to Howl' is the poem that completes the most famous poem of the Beat Generation and one of the most reprinted American poems of the period; its litany of 'holy' is part of the common vocabulary of post-war American poetry, and it is a standard anthology text for the Beats and for the literature of the 1950s.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Howl and Other Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1956); collected in Collected Poems 1947-1980 (1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is holiness - what it is, who confers it and on what - and the poem's answer is everything and everyone, without exception. The second is the body, named explicitly and without euphemism, in a period when that was a legal risk. The third is the Beat generation's counter-theology, which takes the vocabulary of the Catholic upbringing Ginsberg had left and uses it against the institution. The fourth is affirmation as a political act: the poem's 'yes' to everything is a refusal of the American moral order that had made the poem's own subjects criminal.
summary: Every line of the poem begins with the word 'Holy', and the list runs through body parts, people, places and conditions: holy the groin, holy the bum, holy the cock and the cunt, holy the grandmother, holy the screaming infants, holy the indifference of the sidewalks, holy the grinning meat-eaters, holy the solitary apparitions, holy the sea, holy the desert, holy the tongues and the cock and the cunt and the bum and the wombs and the sperm and the spirit. The litany is spoken in the voice of the angel in the first section of Howl, and its function is to declare that everything exists, including the despised and the obscene, and that the whole of it is holy. The poem ends with a fourfold refrain: 'Holy holy holy holy / Holy holy holy holy / Holy holy holy holy / Holy holy holy holy'.
critical_context: Critics read the poem as the theological counterpart to 'Howl', as a Blakean affirmation in the tradition of the prophetic books Ginsberg had been reading, and as an instance of the oral, performance-based poetics of the Beats; its place in the obscenity trial and in the liberalisation of American publishing law is part of its critical history.
research_notes: The 1956 City Lights first edition and the poem's position as the closing poem of the book are recorded from the records of the collection and its history; the exact date of composition is given as the summer of 1955 in the accounts consulted.

title: A Supermarket in California
description: 'A Supermarket in California' is one of the shorter poems in Howl and Other Poems (City Lights, 1956), and it is the most personal of the collection's poems about poetry. It describes the poet walking at night in a supermarket in California, thinking of Walt Whitman, and finding him - or imagining him - among the shoppers and the fruit.
plot_or_argument: 'A Supermarket in California' is an elegy for a poet and for a country, written in the middle of the consumer abundance of the 1950s. Ginsberg's method is to make Whitman a physical presence in the poem - 'childless, lonely old grubber, poking among the meats' - and to let the reader feel the pathos of the great American poet reduced to a shopper, which is also Ginsberg's joke about what America has done with its own tradition. The poem's question, 'Where are we going, Walt Whitman?', is asked in a supermarket, and the answer is that the doors of the supermarket close at dusk and the poets walk out into the night. Ginsberg's Whitman is openly a poet of same-sex desire - the 'grocery boys' are eyed as the poem's speaker eyes them - and the poem's act of inheritance is therefore also an act of outing the tradition, which is the political move the poem makes under its elegiac surface. The closing image of the road, and of García Lorca, extends the lineage beyond the national tradition and makes the poem's company a set of poets who were all, in different ways, outsiders.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem of about twenty-five lines in one stanza, moving from the street to the supermarket to the imagined conversation and out into the night.
meter_and_prosody: Long free-verse lines with colloquial diction and occasional formal address; direct apostrophe to Whitman; a mixture of the specific and the visionary ('neon fruit supermarket', 'the doors close at dusk'); and an ending on an image rather than a statement.
historical_context: Written in Berkeley in 1955 and published in Howl and Other Poems (City Lights, 1956). The poem belongs to the moment when Ginsberg, having left New York and his earlier formal apprenticeship, was writing the poems that made him famous; its address to Whitman places the Beats in a national lineage that the poem simultaneously claims and mourns.
literary_significance: 'A Supermarket in California' is one of the best-known poems of the Beat Generation and a standard anthology text for the period; it is taught as Ginsberg's statement about poetic tradition and as an example of the Beat use of the long line and the direct address.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Howl and Other Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, 1956); collected in Collected Poems 1947-1980 (1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is poetic inheritance - what a young poet can take from a dead one, and what the dead one's America has become. The second is the supermarket as the emblem of a consumer society that has replaced the world Whitman wrote about. The third is same-sex desire, present in the poem's looking and in the company it keeps. The fourth is loneliness, which the poem's ending states without consolation: the poets walk out into the night and the poem cannot say where they are going.
summary: The speaker walks 'down the sidestreets under the trees with a headache self-conscious looking at the full moon' and enters a 'neon fruit supermarket' in 'my hungry fatigues'. He wonders where Whitman is, and the poem imagines him: 'I saw you, Walt Whitman, childless, lonely old grubber, poking among the meats in the refrigerator and eyeing the grocery boys.' The two poets wander the aisles together; Whitman asks about the prices and the family, and the speaker asks him where the lost America has gone. The poem turns at the end to García Lorca, another poet of desire, and closes with the image of the two of them on the road, the speaker following Whitman's 'abandoned' road.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as Ginsberg's negotiation with the American poetic tradition, and discusses the supermarket as a figure for a consumer capitalism that had absorbed the America Whitman wrote; the poem's treatment of Whitman's sexuality has been central to gay and lesbian readings of the period and of Ginsberg's work.
